summary: A 1970 proposal for a simplified Network Control Program protocol by R. Kalin. It suggests a simpler way for hosts to manage network communication. It is a proposal, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A suggestion for a simpler set of rules for how computers talk, because simple rules are easier to build.

questions: what is a crate in the simplified ncp
how does duplex linking simplify protocol
subtitle: A simpler way to build network connections on small computers.

tldr.problem: The proposed NCP protocol at the time was complex, with queues of waiting connection requests and complicated resource allocation. Small computers could not implement it easily.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 60 proposes a simpler NCP using bi-directional connections (duplex links) with message containers called crates. Worst-case buffer requirements are predictable and fixed, eliminating the need for complex queue management.
tldr.outcome: The simplified design was not adopted as the standard NCP, but influenced thinking about protocol simplicity and resource allocation in later network protocols.

facts.label: Buffer states
facts.value: 4 (empty, filled with message, filled with crate, filled with message to send)

today: RFC 60 is not Internet Standard. The actual NCP that emerged took different approaches, but Kalin's emphasis on predictable resource allocation and simple state machines influenced later network design. The idea that protocol should enable worst-case analysis remains important in modern systems.

sections.title: Design Goal
sections.content:
Richard Kalin of MIT Lincoln Laboratory proposed a simpler NCP that could run on very small computers yet scale up to large time-sharing systems. The central idea is that all user-to-user connections should be bi-directional.

In earlier protocol proposals, connections were sometimes one-way, requiring separate paths for requests and replies. Kalin argues this makes protocol unnecessarily complicated. A simple bi-directional connection, called a duplex link, identified by a pair of socket numbers is cleaner and avoids complex flow control problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Two-way connections are simpler than one-way tubes. You ask a question and get an answer back on the same path.

sections.title: Crates and Buffers
sections.content:
Each duplex link carries crates, which are message containers. Buffers at each end of the link hold crates. The key insight is that worst-case buffer requirements can be calculated and are fixed: buffer space needed equals the number of crates in circulation, called the capacity of the link.

Message buffers cycle through four states: empty, filled with a message to unload, filled with an empty crate, and filled with a message to send. This predictable cycle lets the NCP allocate exact amounts of storage upfront, avoiding complex queue overflow and resource errors.
sections.plainLanguage: Send message boxes back and forth. You know exactly how many boxes are in use at any time, so you can allocate storage upfront without a complicated manager.

sections.title: Connection Setup and Closure
sections.content:
To create a connection, the local process asks its NCP to send a RFDL (Request For Duplex Link) over the control link, specifying both socket identifiers. The remote NCP matches incoming RFDL requests against pending listens and replies with an ACDL (Acknowledge Duplex Link), specifying how many crate buffers each end will use.

To close a connection, the NCP sends DEC (decrease) messages to remove empty crates and reclaim buffers. If a user process dies unexpectedly, an ABEND (abnormal end) control message stops transmission and cleans up both ends of the link.
sections.plainLanguage: Say hello with RFDL, the other side says yes with ACDL, and when done send DEC to give back the crates and memory.

sections.title: Enhancements
sections.content:
For larger hosts, the RFC proposes optional extensions including automatic error recovery: if an NCP keeps a copy of each sent message until a reply arrives, it can use STOP and LINQ commands to synchronize the link and identify which messages to retransmit. The host can add crates dynamically with INC commands when it needs more buffer space.

The RFC also notes that larger hosts might allocate more buffers than they physically have, relying on statistics to stay out of trouble. If overload approaches, a host can reduce sending, block local processes, issue DEC messages, or as a last resort, fake errors in messages from remote hosts that support error recovery.
sections.plainLanguage: Fancy additions: automatic replay of lost messages, asking for extra boxes when needed, and tricks to survive overload.

references.text: Crocker, S.D., Postel, J., Newkirk, J. and Kraley, M., "Official protocol proffering", RFC 54, June 1970.
